For lattice spacing and cortex thickness, we modeled values over the total range reported in the feather iridescence database, and number of layers was fixed to 4 (the median in the feather iridescence database). For structures with rods, we modeled structures with a hexagonal packing in addition to the standard laminar configuration (Figure 8B and A, respectively) to represent the diversity present in real structures. Although a square configuration also exists, we did not model this since it has only been recorded in a single genus, the peafowls (Pavo). Table 1 gives a detailed overview of the model settings for each melanosome type. Notice that the melanosome diameter of solid forms is varied in 30 steps, while the diameter of hollow forms is only varied in 10 steps. The thickness of melanin layers is important for determining hue, and hollow forms have two parameters that adjust this value (diameter and hollowness), while solid forms have only one (diameter). To avoid a bias toward greater hue variability in hollow forms due to this effect, we allowed the diameter of solid forms to vary in an equal number of steps as the combined effect of diameter and hollowness in hollow forms (10×3=30).

In total, we ran 4500 simulations, with 900 simulations for each melanosome type.

### Plumage measurements and spectral analysis

We collected spectral measurements of 80 bird species (across 13 orders) for which nanostructures were already known (see references in the feather iridescence database), housed in the American Natural History Museum, New York. Two individuals were used for each species, and all iridescent patches with different color (as perceived by human vision) were measured. In total, 111 unique patches were measured. Spectral measurements were taken directly on the specimen following standard procedures (Andersson and Prager, 2006). Briefly, we used a USB4000 spectrophotometer and a PX-2 xenon light source (Ocean Optics, Dunedin, FL). We measured color over a range of angles (15–135°) using a goniometer, keeping the light source fixed at 75°.

Spectra were analyzed in R v.3.6.1 (R Development Core Team, 2019) using the package pavo (Maia et al., 2013a). All spectral data were first smoothed to remove noise, using locally weighted smoothing (LOESS) and a smoothing parameter of 0.2. We removed negative values by adding the minimal reflectance to the spectrum, and then rescaling this range back to 0–100% reflectance. We then extracted the spectra with maximum total brightness (area under the curve) for each patch. The variability between individuals of each species was assessed using pairwise distances in tetrahedral color space. If the patch measurements for the two individuals were very different in terms of color (separated by >0.1 Euclidean distance in color space), we inspected the spectral measurements to identify possible inaccurate readings. Nine spectra were removed from the data set after this process, leaving a total of 213 spectra used for analysis.

### Calculation of color variables used in analysis

To compare color diversity and color properties of different structures, we focused on five variables: (1) the number of voxels occupied in avian color space, (2) mean color distance in avian color space, (3) color saturation, (4) stimulation of the avian double cones, and (5) peak reflectance. These variables describe color diversity (1–2), color purity (3), perceptual brightness (4), and objective brightness (5), respectively. Peak reflectance is simply the maximum reflectance from each spectrum. Perceptual brightness was modeled as the photon catch from a chicken double cone (Gallus gallus, built-in data in the pavo package; see details above), since current evidence suggests that the double cones mediate achromatic/brightness perception in birds (Hart, 2001; Jones and Osorio, 2004). Saturation and color diversity were based on modeling spectra in avian color space (Stoddard and Prum, 2008). This space represents all the colors a bird can theoretically perceive. Relative cone stimulation was calculated from photon cone catches using cone sensitivity functions in pavo. Bird species vary in their ultraviolet spectral sensitivity; some species have a VS (violet-sensitive) cone type that is maximally sensitive in the violet range while others have a UVS (ultraviolet-sensitive) cone type that is maximally sensitive in the ultraviolet range (Hart, 2001). Because we modeled plumage colors across many phylogenetic groups, we used the sensitivity curves in pavo for an ‘average UVS’ (λmax=372 nm) and ‘average VS’ (λmax=416 nm) type system. Since results in general were similar for a UVS- and VS-type system, we only include analyses based on a VS-type visual model (summary statistics for a UVS-type cone can be found in Supplementary file 1e-f), which is the ancestral condition in birds (Ödeen and Håstad, 2003).

Saturation in tetrahedral color space is simply the distance from the center of the tetrahedron (r vector, as defined by Stoddard and Prum, 2008). For number of voxels occupied, we followed the approach of Delhey, 2015. The tetrahedral color space is divided into 3D pixels (voxels), and then the number of voxels that have at least one data point are counted. The resolution of raster cells was set to 0.1, which gives a total of 236 voxels in tetrahedral color space. Mean color span is a measure of the spread of samples in color space and is calculated as the mean of pairwise Euclidean distances between all samples. This measure is more robust to sample size differences than voxel occupancy, which makes it better suited for comparing the plumage colors in our data set.

### Statistical analysis

To compare iridescent structures recorded in the feather iridescence database (thickness of melanin layers, diameter of interior hollowness, and number of layers), we applied simulation-based phylogenetic analyses of variance (ANOVA), as described by Garland et al., 1993 using the R package phytools (Revell, 2012). Since this function assumes Brownian evolution of traits, we measured phylogenetic signal (Pagel’s lambda) in the traits tested to confirm that this assumption was not violated. All traits tested recorded a high and significant lambda (Supplementary file 1b). To clarify relationships between groups, we also performed phylogenetic pairwise t-tests where necessary (using the R package phytools [Revell, 2012], Supplementary file 1a). Species that had more than one entry in the database (e.g., from multiple studies or multiple patches) were averaged before analysis. For comparison, we also included melanosome diameters from black feathers in some analyses. These data were taken from Li et al., 2012.

We performed a test for multimodality to assess whether solid rods show a binary distribution, following the method described by Fisher and Marron, 2001, which is implemented in the R package modetest (Ameijeiras-Alonso et al., 2018).

To explore how melanosome modifications affect color production, we fitted separate linear models with response variables saturation, avian double cone stimulation, and peak reflectance. Avian double cone stimulation and peak reflectance were log-transformed before inclusion into the models to achieve normally distributed residuals. We used binary predictors to describe the absence/presence of the three melanosome modifications: thin melanin layers (<190 nm), hollowness and platelet shape. We also added the interaction term {hollowness×platelet}, since the optical effect of hollow platelets is not expected to be simply the addition of hollowness and platelet shape. This is because hollow platelets lower the refractive index of melanosome layers by having relatively less melanin in each layer. This property only applies to melanosomes that have both modifications (hollow and platelet) simultaneously. Note that since we have included an interaction term, the variables hollow and platelet are only describing a situation where the interaction is zero (i.e., for hollow rods and solid platelets, respectively).

Spectral data derived from optical simulations were analyzed using multiple linear regressions with the variables described above (summary of results can be found in Supplementary file 1g-i). For plumage data, we also needed to account for phylogenetic relatedness, as well as individual variability in patch color (for each species we had measurements from two individuals). We did this using Bayesian linear mixed models, adding phylogenetic structure and patch as random factors in the model. The phylogeny used was the same as for earlier analyses but pruned to contain only the 80 species in our plumage measurements. We also added a fourth predictor: presence/absence of a photonic crystal (PC). This variable accounts for expected variation in color brightness and saturation that is explained by whether the structure has a single layer of melanosomes or several (in the optical model simulations, all structures had four layers). We used the R package MCMCglmm (Hadfield, 2010) to run our Bayesian model with Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. We ran chains for each model for 50 million generations, with a sampling frequency of 500. The first 50,000 generations were discarded as burnin. We used the default priors for the fixed effects and set an inverse gamma distribution prior for the variance of residuals and random factors. We checked that the analysis had reached a stable phase by visually examining trace plots and checked that autocorrelation values between parameters was low (all <0.1). We also formally tested convergence of the chain using Heidelberg’s and Welch’s convergence diagnostics (all variables passed both tests). Summary of results for each model can be found in Supplementary file 1j-l.

results.result: Iridescent plumage colors in birds are produced by nanostructures in feather barbules consisting of melanosomes and keratin. Brilliant iridescence arises from photonic crystal structures, while weak iridescence is produced by single-layered structures. Melanosomes come in five main types, with thick solid rods likely ancestral to four derived types.
results.evaluation: These claims establish well-documented background knowledge about iridescent feather structures, supported by citations to prior work (particularly Durrer, 1977) and consistent with established optical principles. The classification system and structural mechanisms are clearly defined and widely accepted in the field.

results.result: The authors compiled a feather iridescence database covering 306 bird species across 35 families and 15 orders from 47 studies (1952-2020), representing 37% of avian orders and 14% of families. Data completeness varied, with 92% having information on hollowness/platelet shape but only 61% including melanin layer thickness details.
results.evaluation: The database compilation is clearly described with specific numbers and coverage statistics. The authors acknowledge data limitations and taxonomic biases. This represents a substantial data collection effort that forms the foundation for subsequent analyses.

results.result: Solid rods exhibit a significant bimodal distribution (p<0.001), allowing definition of 'thick solid rods' (≥190 nm diameter) and 'thin solid rods' (<190 nm diameter). Thick solid rods are similar in size to melanosomes in black feathers, supporting their ancestral status, while thin solid rods are considerably modified.
results.evaluation: The bimodal distribution is demonstrated with appropriate statistical testing (C29) and visualized in Figure 4. The 190 nm threshold is data-driven and aligns with theoretical predictions. Comparison with black feather melanosomes (Li et al., 2012) provides independent validation of the ancestral interpretation.

results.result: All four derived melanosome types in brilliant iridescent structures share thin melanin layers (24-139 nm range), achieved through three different mechanisms: decreasing melanosome size directly, hollowing out the interior, or flattening into platelets. All derived types have significantly thinner melanin layers than thick solid rods and black feather melanosomes (p<0.01).
results.evaluation: This is the central finding of the paper, supported by measurements from the database (C33), statistical comparisons (C34), and convergence on the theoretically predicted range (C35, Figure 5). The three mechanisms are clearly demonstrated and the unifying feature of thin melanin layers across all derived types is well-established.

results.result: Based on optical theory for first-order interference peaks in the bird-visible spectrum (300-700 nm), melanin layer thickness should fall between 37.5-206 nm, with maximum reflectance at λ/4. For hollow interiors, air layer thickness should range from 75-350 nm.
results.evaluation: These theoretical predictions are derived from established multilayer optics principles, with clear mathematical reasoning provided. The calculations use appropriate refractive indices for melanin and keratin from the literature. These predictions are subsequently validated by empirical measurements (C35).

results.result: 99% of species with photonic crystals contain melanosomes with thin melanin layers, and over 80% of families (27/32) have evolved this modification. However, 59% of single-layered structures also have thin melanin layers.
results.evaluation: These phylogenetic patterns are clearly quantified from the database and mapped onto the phylogeny (Figure 3). The high prevalence in photonic crystals supports the functional importance of thin melanin layers for brilliant iridescence, though the presence in single-layered structures requires additional explanation (addressed in Discussion).

results.result: Air pocket diameter in hollow melanosomes ranged from 50-251 nm with no significant difference between rods and platelets (p=0.176). Hollow interiors evolved in at least 12 families (34%), platelets in 11 families (31%), but platelets did not allow more layers than rods (p=0.321).
results.evaluation: These findings are supported by phylogenetic ANOVA with appropriate statistical controls. The air pocket size range overlaps with theoretical predictions (75-350 nm), supporting optical tuning. The negative result for platelet layer number (C42) is important for rejecting one hypothesis about platelet function.

results.result: Optical modeling of 4500 structures (900 per melanosome type, all with 4 layers) revealed that thick solid rods are severely constrained in color diversity, while all four derived types with thin melanin layers produce large ranges of saturated colors with similar color diversity. Melanin layer thickness explained the greatest variation in saturation.
results.evaluation: The optical modeling approach is well-described with appropriate parameters (resolution, refractive indices) and systematic variation of structural features. Results are visualized in tetrahedral color space (Figure 6A-E) and quantified with multiple metrics. The standardization to 4 layers allows fair comparison across melanosome types.

results.result: All melanosome modifications increase brightness, with the strongest effect from the interaction of hollowness and platelet shape. The optical model predicts hollow platelets produce the brightest colors, which is supported by plumage data showing significant positive effects of hollowness and platelet shape on brightness.
results.evaluation: The brightness effects are demonstrated in both optical modeling (C47, Figure 6N-O gray points) and empirical plumage measurements (C52, Figure 6N-O black points). The mechanism is explained by refractive index contrast (C113-C114). However, the authors note the hollow platelet effect may be weaker in real structures due to internal honeycomb melanin structure.

results.result: Thin melanin layers (<190 nm) more than double the range of colors producible compared to thick melanin layers, while simultaneously increasing brightness. Above 190 nm, structures produce low saturation and brightness regardless of layer number. Plumage data confirmed near doubling of color diversity for thin versus thick melanin layers.
results.evaluation: This key result integrates optical modeling predictions with empirical validation from plumage measurements (C50, C137). The doubling of color diversity is quantified in Figure 6 and the 190 nm threshold is consistently supported across multiple analyses. The agreement between model and data strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Spectral measurements from 111 patches on 80 species (38 single-layered, 42 photonic crystal) confirmed that photonic crystals produce significantly higher saturation than single-layered structures, independent of melanosome type.
results.evaluation: The plumage data collection is clearly described and analyzed with appropriate Bayesian mixed models accounting for phylogeny and repeated measures. The significant effect of photonic crystal structure (C53) validates a key prediction, though the inability to test thin melanin layer effects in photonic crystals directly (due to lack of thick-rod photonic crystals in the sample) is a limitation.

results.result: The preserved melanosomes from Microraptor plumage have an average diameter of 196 nm, suggesting this feathered theropod exhibited weak rather than brilliant iridescence.
results.evaluation: This application of the 190 nm threshold to fossil data is logical and well-supported by the study's findings. The diameter measurement comes from Li et al., 2012, and the inference follows directly from the established relationship between melanin layer thickness and iridescence type. The authors appropriately caution about inferring structure from fossils.

results.result: Photonic crystals with all four derived melanosome types have similar optical qualities, suggesting variability in melanosome type is strongly influenced by historical factors rather than specific optical functions. Different structures often have independent evolutionary origins within and across families.
results.evaluation: This interpretation is well-supported by the optical modeling showing similar color diversity across derived types (C45, C51) and phylogenetic evidence of independent origins (C61, C62, Figure 3A). The conclusion that historical contingency explains diversity is reasonable given the functional equivalence demonstrated.

results.result: Interpatch variability in melanosome type occurs only in birds-of-paradise and hummingbirds, groups with exceptionally high rates of color evolution and typically >9 melanosome layers. Color production is similar among patches with different melanosome types in these groups.
results.evaluation: The observation of interpatch variability is documented with appropriate citations (C63, C65). The association with high color evolution rates is supported by multiple references (C67). The interpretation that variability reflects high evolutionary rates rather than optical tuning is reasonable given that >9 layers already achieve near-maximal reflectance (C68, C135) and color production is similar across types (C69).

results.result: The authors propose two evolutionary paths to brilliant iridescence from ancestral single-layered thick solid rod structures: Path 1 involves evolving modified melanosomes first (supported by common single-layered structures with modified melanosomes), while Path 2 involves evolving photonic crystals first (supported by hexagonal hollow rod structures in groups with thick solid rod ancestors).
results.evaluation: This evolutionary hypothesis is speculative and based on limited phylogenetic sampling. While the database provides some support for both paths (C74, C75), the authors acknowledge that "very few clades are sampled in sufficient detail to draw inferences about transitions." Testing these hypotheses would require detailed phylogenetic analysis within clades showing repeated transitions, which is not provided. This represents an interesting framework for future work rather than a well-supported conclusion.

results.result: Optical modeling used MIT MEEP software with phylogenies from Jetz et al., 2012, resolution of 80 pixels/μm, melanin extinction coefficient k=0.1, keratin refractive index n=1.56, and melanin refractive index n=2.
results.evaluation: The computational methods are clearly described with specific parameter values. However, the authors acknowledge these are approximations and that refractive indices vary across wavelengths in reality. The resolution provides adequate sampling (12 points per 300 nm wave). While simplified, the parameters are reasonable and based on published values.

results.result: Saturation is low for all single-layered structures except hollow platelets, though data for hollow platelets come mainly from African starlings. Single-layered structures behave differently from photonic crystals and deserve further study.
results.evaluation: The exception for hollow platelets in single-layered structures (C100) is intriguing but the authors appropriately note the taxonomic bias (C101). Whether this represents a general phenomenon or is specific to starlings cannot be determined from current data. The call for further study (C102) is warranted given this uncertainty.

results.result: Prior work by Maia et al., 2013b showed that evolution of hollow/platelet melanosomes in African starlings was associated with expansions in color diversity and brilliance increases. Eliason et al., 2013 showed hollow rods increase brightness compared to solid rods.
results.evaluation: These are accurate summaries of cited prior work that provide important context for the current study. The current work extends these findings by showing that thin melanin layers, rather than hollowness or platelet shape per se, are the key unifying feature.

results.result: Melanin influences feather mechanical properties and bacterial degradation resistance. Structures with derived melanosomes have converged on shared melanin layer thickness ranges, suggesting melanin content differences may not be large.
results.evaluation: The non-optical functions of melanin are established by citations (C70, C71). The inference about similar melanin content (C72) is reasonable given the convergence on similar thickness ranges (Figure 5), though the authors appropriately note this has never been directly measured and suggest it as future work.

results.result: For weak iridescence in single-layered structures, keratin cortex thickness controls interference color, making melanin layer thickness largely irrelevant. This explains why thick solid rods persist in single-layered structures with no selection pressure to decrease melanin thickness.
results.evaluation: This explanation for the persistence of thick solid rods in single-layered structures is well-reasoned and supported by citations about thin film optics (C105). The logic is sound: if melanosomes only delimit the keratin layer rather than participating in interference, their thickness would not affect color production (C118-C119).
